288.title: The Krishna in the ballast clay
288.hook: a ship in a storm, a monk on the shore, and a lump of clay with Krishna inside
288.carry: dvaita: God, souls and world are truly two
288.howItsDone: Followers of Madhva, the Madhva Vaishnavas, centered on Udupi in Karnataka, worship Krishna as Vishnu, study Madhva's commentaries, and understand the soul as eternally distinct from and dependent on God.

segments.voice: Last week: Advaita, and the line five sheaths, and the one who sees them. Clay and pots, the rope and the snake, and Shankara singing worship Govinda. Today, the teachers who read the same texts and said: two.
screen: `FIVE SHEATHS, AND THE ONE WHO SEES THEM.`

segments.voice: A trading ship is caught in a storm off the coast of Karnataka, near Udupi. A monk standing on the beach, the story goes, waves his cloth, and the ship comes safely in. The grateful captain offers him anything on board. The monk asks for one thing: a big lump of pale clay the sailors had been using as ballast. They break it open, and inside is an image of Krishna, holding a churning rope. That image, tradition says, is the one still worshiped in the Krishna temple at Udupi today. The monk was Madhva.
screen: `A SHIP IN A STORM OFF UDUPI.` → `A LUMP OF BALLAST CLAY.` → `KRISHNA INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Tradition places Madhva in the thirteenth century. He founded a school of Vedanta called Tattvavada, the teaching of what's real. Today it's usually called Dvaita: two. Where Shankara said not two, Madhva said two, clearly and forever. God is one reality. You are another. The world is another, and it's real, not a snake on a rope. Madhva spelled out five differences that never go away: God from souls, God from matter, each soul from every other soul, souls from matter, and each bit of matter from every other. God, for Madhva, is Vishnu, and only God is independent. Everything else, you, me, the clay, depends on God, moment by moment. Not as a snake depends on a rope, a mistake. As a child depends on a parent: really there, really held. And here's what that gives devotion. Madhva's followers put it this way: if you and God were finally one, love would be only a stage on the way. Advaitins answer that differently, as you heard. For Madhva, the difference is the truth, so the love can last. Even a freed soul doesn't dissolve into God. It stays itself, in God's presence, loving and serving. The lover and the beloved stay two, and the space between them isn't a wall. It's where the love happens. That's Dvaita, and it's why so many Hindu devotees call themselves God's servant, dasa, and never expect to become God. Advaita and Dvaita are both alive today, and neither is ranked here.
screen: `TATTVAVADA: WHAT'S REAL.` · `FIVE DIFFERENCES, FOREVER.` · `ONLY GOD IS INDEPENDENT.` · `FREED, AND STILL TWO.` · then, large: `DVAITA: GOD, SOULS AND WORLD ARE TRULY TWO.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you love who is really, stubbornly not you: they laugh at different things, want different things. Notice that the love lives exactly in that difference; if they were you, there'd be no one to love. Feel the space between you as room, not distance. If you pray, turn that same warmth toward God, as other than you, and near.
Dvaita, two. God, souls and the world are really distinct, only God is independent, and the freed soul stays itself, loving God forever.
Your line: dvaita, God, souls and world are truly two. A real God, a real you, and room between for love. Day two eighty-eight, done.

289.title: Ramanuja on the temple tower
289.hook: a teacher gives him a secret mantra; he climbs the temple tower and shouts it to the town
289.carry: the whole world is God's body
289.tomorrow: The gopis and the learned messenger
289.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas, followers of Ramanuja, worship Vishnu with Lakshmi, especially at temples like Srirangam, recite the Alvars' Tamil hymns alongside Sanskrit texts, and practice prapatti, surrender to God, as the heart of the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Madhva's Dvaita, the Krishna in the ballast clay. Your line: dvaita, God, souls and world are truly two. Today, a third answer, from a teacher who came before Madhva.

A young scholar named Ramanuja walks, tradition says, eighteen times to the house of an old teacher, asking for a sacred mantra. South India, around nine hundred years ago. Seventeen times he's turned away. The eighteenth time, the teacher gives it, with a warning: keep this secret. Tell no one, or you'll go to hell. Ramanuja walks straight to the temple, climbs the tall gateway tower, and calls the mantra out to everyone in the street below. The teacher is furious. Ramanuja says: if I go to hell and all these people are saved, I'll gladly go.
screen: `EIGHTEEN WALKS TO A TEACHER.` → `KEEP THIS SECRET.` → `SHOUTED FROM THE TEMPLE TOWER.`

segments.voice: The teacher, the story goes, embraced him. Ramanuja became the great teacher of the Sri Vaishnava tradition, centered at the temple of Srirangam, and he gave Vedanta a third answer. Not Shankara's not two. Not quite Madhva's two, which came about a century later. His school is called Vishishtadvaita: not two, but qualified. One reality, with real distinctions inside it. His picture is the body and the soul. You live in your body and guide it from inside. The body is real, not a snake on a rope. But it isn't independent either. It's yours. For Ramanuja, the whole universe, every soul and every grain of matter, is the body of God. And God, Vishnu, Narayana, is the soul of it all. He found this in the Upanishads, where the sage Yajnavalkya describes the inner controller. Paraphrased: the one who dwells in the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who guides the earth from within: that is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. For Ramanuja, you're really you, forever. God is really God. And yet God is closer to you than your own body is. That's why his tradition sees love and surrender to God as the path. The freed soul doesn't vanish into God. It enjoys God, as God's own. So for Ramanuja's followers the river, the stranger on the bus, your own hands, aren't a trick. The whole world is God's body.

segments.voice: Feel your body from the inside: your hands, your chest rising, the weight of your legs, really yours. Then try Ramanuja's picture: the room, the city, the trees, the people you love, all one great body, with a life at its center that lives in you too. If you pray, rest in that nearness; if not, feel the body and the room, and breathe.
Vishishtadvaita, not two but qualified. One reality: the world and souls are God's body, God is their inner self, and the soul stays itself, loving God.
Your line: the whole world is God's body. Really you, really God, and very near. That's two eighty-nine.

290.title: The gopis and the learned messenger
290.hook: I want to taste sugar, not become sugar
290.carry: bhakti needs two: a lover and a beloved
290.howItsDone: In Vaishnava devotional traditions, teachers often explain that bhakti depends on the relationship between the devotee and God, and the gopis' love for Krishna in the Bhagavata Purana is held up as its model.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramanuja on the temple tower, and the world as God's body. Your line: the whole world is God's body. Today, the question underneath all of this.

In Calcutta, the mystic Ramakrishna, whose student Vivekananda you met a few weeks ago, used to repeat a line from an old Bengali devotional song. People asked him about merging into God, becoming one with the absolute, and he'd answer, more or less: I don't want to become sugar. I want to taste sugar. It's a joke, and an argument. If you become the sugar, who's left to enjoy the sweetness?
screen: `CALCUTTA, RAMAKRISHNA.` → `I DON'T WANT TO BECOME SUGAR.` → `I WANT TO TASTE IT.`

segments.voice: This is the heart of bhakti, devotion, and the devotional schools make their case in that one line. Love, they say, needs two: a lover and a beloved, someone to give and someone to receive, someone to sing and someone to hear. Take away the difference, and you may have peace, or bliss, but not love the way a mother loves a child, or a friend a friend. The Bhagavata Purana tells a story about this. Krishna has left the village where he grew up, and the cowherd women who loved him, the gopis, are heartbroken. He sends his friend Uddhava, a learned man, to comfort them, and Uddhava comforts them with philosophy. Krishna is everywhere, he says; he's the self of all; you're never really apart from him. The gopis answer, paraphrased: that's lovely. We want Krishna. Not the self of all. Him. His flute, his laugh, his face. Uddhava, humbled, says he'd gladly be a bush or a creeper in their village, just to be touched by the dust of their feet. Other teachers explored the ground between. Nimbarka taught difference and non-difference at once. In Bengal, Chaitanya's followers called it inconceivable: one with God and different from God, both, beyond what the mind can hold. Now, fairly. Advaita teachers honor devotion too, as you heard with Bhaja Govindam, and some of them say love, fully ripened, dissolves into oneness. The devotional schools say love, fully ripened, stays two and grows forever. Hindus hold both, side by side. Nobody here has to pick.
screen: `LOVE NEEDS TWO.` · `THE GOPIS WANT KRISHNA, NOT A THEORY.` · `ONE AND DIFFERENT, BEYOND THOUGHT.` · `TWO VIEWS, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `BHAKTI NEEDS TWO: A LOVER AND A BELOVED.`

segments.voice: Hindus often offer food to God before they eat, then receive it back as prasad, a gift. Try it with something nearby, a sip of tea, a raisin, a square of chocolate, or remember one. Hold it a moment and offer it in your heart to God, or simply say thank you. Then taste it slowly, and notice two things: the sweetness, and the one enjoying it. That's Ramakrishna's sugar.
Gopis, the cowherd women who loved Krishna. Love needs a lover and a beloved; to taste sugar, you can't become it.
Your line: bhakti needs two, a lover and a beloved. Someone has to be there to taste the sugar. Until tomorrow.

291.title: Kanaka's window
291.hook: a shepherd poet isn't let into the temple, so he sings from behind the wall
291.carry: God turns toward the devotee left outside
291.howItsDone: At the Udupi Krishna temple, devotees view Krishna through a small latticed window, and Kanaka's window on the west wall is honored as a place of pilgrimage; the Haridasa songs of Kanakadasa and Purandaradasa are sung across Karnataka and in Carnatic music.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gopis, who wanted Krishna, not a theory, and Ramakrishna's sugar. Your line: bhakti needs two, a lover and a beloved. Today, back to Udupi.

Visit the Krishna temple at Udupi today, the one with the image from the ballast clay, and you'll notice something odd. You don't see Krishna face to face through a big open doorway. You look at him through a small latticed window, nine little openings in a silver frame. And on the outside of the temple wall, on the west side, there's another window with a story attached, and a shrine to a poet. The story is about a shepherd who wasn't allowed in.
screen: `THE KRISHNA TEMPLE AT UDUPI.` → `SEEN THROUGH A SMALL WINDOW.` → `A SHEPHERD WHO WASN'T LET IN.`

segments.voice: His name was Kanakadasa, a poet from the Kuruba community, shepherds, in Karnataka. He belonged to the Haridasas, the servants of Hari, who took Madhva's teaching out of Sanskrit and into Kannada songs people could sing in the fields. His teacher, the Madhva scholar Vyasatirtha, is remembered as loving him. But when Kanaka came to Udupi to see Krishna, the temple authorities of the time, the story goes, wouldn't let him in because of his birth. So he went around to the back, stood outside the west wall, and sang, and sang, to a Krishna he couldn't see. Tradition says the wall cracked open, and the image inside turned around to face him. The crack became a window, still called Kanaka's window, and the image, they say, faces west to this day. Here's the teaching inside the story. The temple kept a gate; God didn't. In bhakti, God turns toward love, not birth. And the two stay two: Kanaka is still Kanaka, Krishna still Krishna. But the wall becomes a window. There's a gentler story about him too. His teacher gave each student a banana and said: eat it where no one can see you. Everyone came back having eaten theirs in some hidden corner. Kanaka came back with his uneaten. Wherever I went, he said, Krishna was watching. Two, always, and never out of sight. Pilgrims still stop at Kanaka's window, and his own songs ask what birth has to do with God.

segments.voice: Picture yourself outside a wall, the way Kanaka stood: maybe a real place where you felt unwelcome, maybe just the sense that God, or meaning, is somewhere you can't see. Sing inwardly, or just long, and picture a small window opening, and something on the other side turning toward you. If you pray, speak through that window; if not, stay by the wall, unhurried.

292.title: The monkey and the kitten
292.hook: a baby monkey clings to its mother, a kitten is carried in its mother's mouth, and Ramanuja's followers asked which one you are
292.carry: prapatti: taking refuge in God's grace
292.tomorrow: You are that, or you are his?
292.howItsDone: Many Sri Vaishnavas formally take refuge through a rite called samashrayana, given by a teacher, and recite the dvaya mantra and Gita 18.66 daily; the northern (Vadakalai) and southern (Tenkalai) lineages are often told apart by the shape of the namam, the mark worn on the forehead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kanaka's window: the shepherd poet outside the wall at Udupi. Your line: God turns toward the devotee left outside. Today, back to Ramanuja's people.

A mother monkey leaps from branch to branch. Her baby rides along, holding on to her belly with its own small hands. A mother cat moves her kitten another way. She picks it up by the scruff of its neck, and the kitten just hangs there, loose, carried. Two babies, two mothers, two ways of getting across. In South India, Ramanuja's later followers argued over these two animals, because the question underneath them is a big one. When God saves a soul, how much does the soul hold on?
screen: `A BABY MONKEY CLINGS.` → `A KITTEN IS CARRIED.` → `HOW MUCH DOES THE SOUL HOLD ON?`

segments.voice: You met Ramanuja a few days ago, on the temple tower, with the world as God's body. Today, the heart of how his followers practice: prapatti, surrender, taking refuge. Not giving up. Turning to God the way a child turns to a parent, and letting yourself be held. Sri Vaishnavas say Ramanuja himself, at the temple of Srirangam, offered a prose prayer of surrender before Vishnu and Lakshmi, and they still recite it. They treasure a verse near the end of the Gita, which they call the final verse. Krishna says, roughly: let go of every other support, take refuge in me alone, I will free you from every wrong, do not grieve. Later came the question from the hook. One lineage, later called the northern school, taught with the baby monkey: grace carries you, and you also hold on, with your own small effort. The other, the southern school, taught with the kitten: grace does everything, and even your holding on is a gift. Both lineages trace themselves to Ramanuja, and both are alive today. This path doesn't settle it. But both pictures share something: a mother and a child. Two. Surrender only makes sense if there's someone to surrender to. Advaita would say that in the end there's only one. Ramanuja's people say the soul is held, forever, and never stops being the one who is held. That's devotion needing difference. 293.title: You are that, or you are his?
293.hook: a proud son comes home after twelve years of study, and his father gives him three words: tat tvam asi
293.howItsDone: Followers of Madhva, often called Madhvas, worship Vishnu as supreme; the Krishna temple at Udupi, which tradition says Madhva founded, is a center of their tradition, and pilgrims still look through Kanaka's window.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prapatti: the baby monkey and the kitten, both held. Your line: prapatti, taking refuge in God's grace. Today, back to Madhva, and three famous words.

A boy named Shvetaketu leaves home at twelve to study the Vedas. At twenty-four, the Chandogya Upanishad says, he comes back proud, sure he's learned it all. His father, Uddalaka, asks one question: did you ask for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, and the unknown becomes known? The son has no idea. So the father starts over, with a lump of clay, a seed, salt dissolved in water. And again and again he ends with three words: tat tvam asi.
screen: `HOME AT TWENTY-FOUR, AND PROUD.` → `CLAY, A SEED, SALT IN WATER.` → `TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: Tat tvam asi: you are that. Shankara's school hears it as the self and Brahman, not two. Five days ago you met Madhva's five differences. Today, the reason underneath them. Madhva sorts everything that is into two kinds. One is svatantra, independent, depending on nothing. Only God, Vishnu, is that. Everything else is paratantra, dependent: every soul, all of matter, even the goddess Lakshmi, his tradition says. All of it is real, and all of it leans on God. His followers sum it up in a phrase: Hari sarvottama, Vishnu is supreme. So how does his school hear the father's three words? Some of its teachers hear tasya tvam asi, you are his: you belong to that. Others divide the sounds differently and hear atat tvam asi, you are not that. Same Sanskrit, a different ear. For Madhva, if the soul were secretly God, worship would be a kind of pretending. If God is truly other, and the soul truly depends on him, then love has somewhere to go. Think back to Kanaka's window: a real distance, and a God who turns to cross it. Advaita teachers would say the distance is finally unreal. Madhva's followers say it's where love lives. Both are Hindu, and both are still taught. So when one Hindu says I am that, and another says I am his, they're quoting the same line.

segments.voice: Let yourself feel small for a moment, in a good way: not ashamed, just small, the way you feel under a big sky, with so much bigger than you, the day ahead, the people you love, whatever holds it all. Let the distance be fine; Kanakadasa sang from outside the wall. If you pray, turn toward God from exactly where you are; if you don't, face toward something larger, and rest.
Svatantra, independent, depending on nothing. Only God is svatantra; souls and the world are real, different, and depend on him. The distance isn't a problem to solve. It's where love goes.

294.title: Shankara at his mother's side
294.hook: a boy in a crocodile's jaws makes his mother a promise, and keeps it years later at her bedside
294.carry: God beyond form, and God to love
294.howItsDone: Many Hindus pray both ways: with a name and a form, through japa, puja and song to Krishna, Shiva, the Goddess or Rama, and in silent meditation on Brahman beyond form; the schools of Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva and Chaitanya are all still taught in monasteries and lineages today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, svatantra: only God is independent, and tat tvam asi heard as you are his. Today, the last of these two weeks, and the teacher of not two at his mother's side.

A boy is bathing in a river in Kerala when a crocodile grabs his leg. His mother is on the bank. He calls to her: let me become a monk, now, and I can die a monk. Terrified, she says yes. The crocodile, the story says, lets go. The boy is Shankara, who will grow up to teach not two. Before he leaves home, he makes her a promise: when your time comes, wherever I am, I'll be there.
screen: `A CROCODILE IN THE RIVER.` → `LET ME BECOME A MONK.` → `I'LL BE THERE WHEN YOUR TIME COMES.`

segments.voice: Years later, the traditional lives of Shankara say, he feels her calling and comes home. She's dying. And the great teacher of not two does what he knows best: he speaks to her of Brahman beyond every form, no shape, no name, pure being. She can't hold it. She wants a God she can picture. So he sings to her instead, hymns to God with a form, and tradition says that as he sang to Vishnu, she died at peace. Here's the teaching. Hindus speak of Brahman in two ways: nirguna, without qualities, beyond every form, and saguna, with qualities, God with a face and a name you can love. Shankara's school says the formless is the final truth, and still honors worship of God with a face as real and good on the way. A short hymn credited to him, the Shatpadi, six verses, says it in one line, paraphrased: even when difference is gone, Lord, I am yours; you are not mine. The wave belongs to the ocean, never the ocean to the wave. Look at the map you've walked. Shankara: not two. Ramanuja: one, with the world as God's body. Madhva: two, forever. Chaitanya: one and different, beyond thought. The tradition kept them all. So one Hindu home can hold a father sitting in silence with not two, and a grandmother singing to Krishna. God beyond form, and God to love.
screen: `A PROMISE KEPT AT HER BEDSIDE.` · `NIRGUNA: BEYOND EVERY FORM.` · `SAGUNA: GOD WITH A FACE.` · `THE WAVE BELONGS TO THE OCEAN.` · then, large: `GOD BEYOND FORM, AND GOD TO LOVE.`

segments.voice: Two ways Hindus pray, side by side. First, with a name: say one name of God slowly a few times, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, Rama, whichever is yours, the way families do japa on a string of beads. Then let the name go, and sit in silence, no picture, no word, just being here. Go back and forth once or twice. If you don't pray, say a word that matters to you, then rest in the quiet after it.
Shatpadi, the six-verse hymn credited to Shankara: even when difference is gone, I am yours. Nirguna and saguna, God beyond form and God to love: the tradition keeps both.
